description: We are Team I.S.R.O., a group of six enthusiastic members passionate about technology, innovation, and space exploration. Our project, Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, aims to make space education fun through interactive astronaut training activities, mission simulations, and challenges. We welcome teammates skilled in coding, robotics, designing, research, and creative problem-solving. Together, we aim to inspire young minds to explore space and become future astronauts. 🚀
summary: Junior Space Astronaut Mission is an interactive educational game designed to help children learn about space and the solar system through fun exploration and exciting missions. Players become junior astronauts, explore all eight planets using interactive 3D models, complete challenges, solve puzzles, and answer quizzes. With the help of an AI companion named NOVA, children learn interesting facts about planets, space, and astronomy while earning rewards and unlocking new missions. The main goal is to make learning about space simple, fun, and engaging. 🚀🌍

Little Space Explorer — Project

Description

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Little Space Explorer is a kid-

friendly, browser-based space game with

five activities, all reachable from one

home screen:

1. Planet Hop — an animated solar

system. Tapping a planet opens a large

illustrated view with one short fact.

The system is drawn on an HTML canvas

with sun-directed lighting, depth-

scaled orbits, a rotating asteroid

belt, planet trails, and Earth's moon.

2. Galaxy Spin — a three-step zoom-out:

Earth, to the Solar System, to theMilky Way. The galaxy layer can be spun

by dragging.

3. Space Quiz — five picture questions

with instant, encouraging feedback.

4. Star Catch — a 20-second reflex

game: tap falling stars, catch 10 to

win.

5. Moon Match — a memory game with six

matching pairs.

Completing each activity earns a star.

Progress (which planets were visited,

best scores) is stored in localStorage,

so it survives a reload. All art is

generated in code — the planets are

canvas-drawn gradients, bands, craters,

and rings, not image files — and sound

is synthesized at runtime with the Web

Audio API. Short spoken narration uses

the browser's built-in speech synthesis and can be muted with one button.

BENEFITS

- Zero setup, zero dependencies. No

frameworks, no build step, no external

assets or network requests — three

files (index.html, styles.css, game.js)

open directly in any modern browser,

even offline.

- Tiny footprint. About 166 KB total,

so it loads instantly and runs on low-

end phones.

- One-tap UI for pre-readers. Every

action is a tap on a large, high-

contrast target; text is deliberately

short; narration and sound do most of

the teaching.

- Gentle failure. No punishing

countdowns, no lives lost, no harsh

buzzers — feedback is soft tones and a

retry.

- Accessible by default. Full aria-

label, aria-pressed, and aria-hidden

coverage, semantic sections, keyboard-

reachable buttons, and a prefers-

reduced-motion rule that disables

animation for users who need it.- Responsive. Separate layout rules for

phones, tablets, and desktops,

including short-screen and landscape

cases.

INTENDED IMPACT

The goal is to make a child's first

encounter with astronomy playful,

social, and screen-time-friendly —

something a 4-to-8-year-old can use

alone or with a parent, in a waiting

room or on a bus, without ads,

accounts, or internet. Because it can

run from a phone on the local network (

the included server serves HTTP and

HTTPS on one port), a parent can set it

up once and hand a tablet to a child

with nothing else reachable. It also

serves as a small, readable reference

for what a complete, polished game can

be with plain web technology — useful

for classrooms and beginner coding

clubs.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, AND

SOFTWARE

- Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla

JavaScript (ES6+). No libraries or

frameworks.

- Browser APIs: Canvas 2D (starfield,solar system, galaxy, particles), Web

Audio API (oscillator-based UI and

reward sounds), Speech Synthesis API (

narration), localStorage (progress),

Pointer Events, and devicePixelRatio

for crisp rendering on high-density

screens.

- Server: a ~95-line Python 3 script (

serve.py) built on http.server and

socketserver that peeks at the first

byte of each connection and wraps it in

TLS when it sees a handshake, so http:/

/ and https:// both work on the same

port. A self-signed certificate is

generated locally with openssl, and

start.sh prints the LAN address to use

from another device.

- Hardware and OS: developed and tested

on an Android phone in Termux, using

Python 3, OpenSSL, and the phone's

browser for testing — a deliberately

constrained environment that doubled as

a low-end performance test.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- Everything is drawn, nothing is

downloaded. Each planet has a hand-

authored palette and rendering style —

banded Jupiter, swirled Venus, cratered

Mercury and Moon, icy Uranus, Neptune's

dark spot, and Saturn's rings drawn

twice so they pass in front of and

behind the planet. The asteroid belt,galaxy dust, and starfield are

procedural, with twinkle, parallax, and

shooting stars.

- Teaching through motion, not text.

The solar system's lighting comes from

the Sun, so the day side of every

planet always faces it; the zoom-out

tells the story of scale without a

single paragraph, while the Moon orbits

Earth as Earth orbits the Sun.

- Feel as a feature. Eased camera

moves, spring-like button feedback,

particle bursts on every star earned,

and a synthesized sound palette give it

the polish of a commercial app while

staying dependency-free.

- Design for the smallest user. Big tap

targets, one idea per screen, short

words, and a star that appears exactly

once per achievement.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

- Age and reading level — pre-readers

must be able to play, hence narration,icons, and one-line facts.

- Device constraints — low-end Android

phones: pixel ratio capped at 2,

particle and star counts reduced on

narrow screens, and short-screen media

queries.

- Accessibility — screen-reader labels,

keyboard operation, reduced-motion

support, and high contrast in a dark

theme.

- Privacy and safety — no accounts, no

analytics, no ads, no network calls;

progress never leaves the device.

- Cost and sustainability — plain web

files will still run years from now;

nothing to update or pay for.

- Classroom and home deployment — an

offline-capable local server with sane

LAN defaults, plus an easy switch to

keep it phone-only.

- Fairness in the mini-games —

forgiving hit boxes, no punishing

timers, and endless retries so a young

child never hits a dead end.
